title: Abraham Lincoln Wins a Four-Way Presidential Election
summary: On November 6, 1860, American voters chose among four candidates for president, and Abraham Lincoln won 180 electoral votes with about 40 percent of the popular vote.

body.text: A Country Divided Over Slavery

On November 6, 1860, American voters chose a president at a time the National Park Service describes as the eve of civil war. The main issue was slavery and whether it should spread into new territories and states. About 31.5 million people lived in the United States, and about 6.9 million of them, just under 45 percent of the voting-age population, were eligible to vote. Women could not vote, and in most states neither could minorities. Of those who were eligible, 81 percent cast a ballot. There was no national voting standard, so the rules for voting varied by state, and a voter's ballot was a ticket printed for a single party.
Four Candidates, Four Parties

According to the Miller Center, the Republican Party met in Chicago in May and nominated Abraham Lincoln of Illinois on the third ballot. Its platform opposed extending slavery into the territories. The Democratic Party split after Southern delegates walked out of its convention in Charleston, South Carolina, in a dispute over a federal slave code for the territories. Its northern wing nominated Stephen Douglas of Illinois, who wanted residents of the territories to decide the question themselves. Southern Democrats nominated John Breckinridge of Kentucky, who wanted slavery protected in the territories by federal law. John Bell of Tennessee ran for the Constitutional Union Party, which put forward no platform beyond the Constitution and the preservation of the Union.
The Campaign

The Miller Center reports that Douglas was the only major candidate to campaign actively, travelling from New England to the Deep South. Breckinridge gave a single speech, Bell did not campaign in public, and Lincoln stayed in Springfield, Illinois, receiving visitors. Republican supporters held torchlight parades, and the Miller Center says William L. Yancey, a Southern Democrat, warned Northern audiences that Lincoln's election would bring secession.
The Results

The American Presidency Project at the University of California, Santa Barbara, lists 1,867,198 votes for Lincoln, or 39.8 percent. Douglas received 1,379,434 votes (29.4 percent), Breckinridge 854,248 (18.2 percent) and Bell 591,658 (12.6 percent). Other compilations give slightly different totals. In the Electoral College, Lincoln won 180 votes, Breckinridge 72, Bell 39 and Douglas 12, so Douglas placed second in the popular vote and last in the Electoral College. By the figures above, the votes for Douglas and Bell together came to about 104,000 more than Lincoln's.
After the Election
The National Park Service says that discontent in the South spread immediately. Seven states in the Deep South had withdrawn from the Union before Lincoln took office in March 1861.

title: Rutgers and Princeton Play the First College Football Game
summary: On November 6, 1869, Rutgers beat Princeton 6–4 in New Brunswick, New Jersey, in the game Rutgers counts as the first college football game.

body.text: A Challenge From Rutgers

Rutgers describes the game as the first college football game. Its roots, in Rutgers' account, lie in an earlier loss: three years before, Princeton's baseball team had beaten Rutgers 40–2. Rutgers students, led by the Rev. C.D. Hartranft, who headed a Dutch Reformed congregation in New Brunswick, formed a football team, and Princeton formed one as well. Rutgers captain William J. Leggett wrote a challenge for a series of three games, and Princeton captain William S. Gummere accepted right away. History.com notes that the two schools, about 20 miles apart, already had an intense rivalry, including a dispute over a Revolutionary War cannon.
The Rules

Princeton's team travelled to New Brunswick by train for the first game on November 6, 1869, and the Rutgers players met them and showed them around town. The captains set the rules. Each side fielded 25 players, who could hit the ball with their fists or hands as well as kick it. Players had names for their roles, such as fielders and bull dogs. The field measured 360 by 225 feet, with goals 24 feet wide, and holding or tripping an opponent was banned. The first team to score six games, or points, would win. History.com adds that the ball was a soccer ball and that the game looked more like rugby than modern football.
The Game

Play began at 3 p.m. on a chilly day on a plot behind the College Avenue Gymnasium, and about 100 spectators watched. Rutgers players wore scarlet scarves as turbans. Princeton players wore street clothes and some athletic wear, and Princeton had not yet adopted orange and black. Neither team had protective gear. Leggett told his players to keep their kicks short and low, and the student newspaper, the Targum, described the play as running, shouting and kicking. George Dixon and Stephen Gano scored Rutgers' first point. Rutgers led 4–2 at one stage, Princeton drew level, and Rutgers then scored twice to win 6–4. Afterwards the two teams shared supper and songs, with Rutgers as host.
The Rematch

A week later the teams met again in Princeton, on a pasture used as a field. Princeton won 8–0, helped, Rutgers says, by loud home fans and home-team rules. The teams again shared a meal. The third game was never played. Princeton had outscored Rutgers 12–6 across the two games, and under a disputed claim Princeton was named national champion for 1869, although each team had won one game. According to Rutgers, the rivalry resumed the following year and lasted until 1980. In 2019, to mark 150 years of college football, Rutgers theater students re-enacted the first game, according to History.com.

title: The Canadian Corps Attacks and Takes Passchendaele Village
summary: On November 6, 1917, the Canadian Corps attacked at 6 a.m. and captured the village of Passchendaele in Belgium during the Third Battle of Ypres.

body.text: Ordered North

The Commonwealth War Graves Commission (CWGC) records that the Canadian Corps received orders on 9 October 1917 to move north into Belgium. Army command had called a temporary halt to the offensive on 13 October but decided to continue in order to secure the dry ground of Passchendaele Ridge, and the Canadians were brought in as fresh troops. About nine days after the order they took over from Australian troops facing Passchendaele village. The corps commander, Arthur Currie, noted in his diary on 17 October that the battlefield looked bad, with no salvage done and very few of the dead buried.
Preparing the Ground

British and Canadian personnel improved the supply lines behind the Canadian front. The CWGC says the ground held by the Canadian Corps alone was served by over two miles of plank roadway and above 4,000 yards of tramway, much of it laid under fire. German positions were mapped, and guns and ammunition were brought forward.
Attacks of 26 and 30 October

The first attack began at 5:40 a.m. on 26 October behind a creeping artillery barrage, through rain and mud on both sides of the flooded Ravebeek stream. It had mixed success: some objectives were missed, but the Canadians gained a foothold on Bellevue Spur and the southern part of the ridge. A second attack on 30 October took most of its objectives and placed outposts about 100 yards from the edge of the village.
6 November

The attack on Passchendaele village began at 6 a.m. on 6 November. The CWGC describes bayonet fighting in the ruins, with cellars and dugouts cleared by Lewis gun fire and grenades. By mid-afternoon all Canadian objectives had been reached and more than 500 German prisoners taken, and by 7:30 p.m. the front was comparatively quiet. Veterans Affairs Canada says the 5th Canadian Infantry Brigade took and passed the village that day after heavy fighting in unfavourable weather. Private James Peter Robertson of the 27th Battalion was awarded the Victoria Cross for what he did that morning, and he died later the same day.
Casualties and Withdrawal

A final attack on 10 November reached its objectives, but British units on the left were forced back by a German counter-attack. The Canadian Corps left the line on 14 November. A Canadian memorial in the area carries an inscription saying that the corps advanced across a valley then described as a treacherous morass and captured and held the ridge, Veterans Affairs Canada reports. The CWGC records more than 12,400 Canadian casualties, wounded, missing or killed, between 26 October and 11 November, about 4,000 of them dead. Separately, the CWGC commemorates more than 3,700 Canadians who died in Belgium during the battle, from 26 October to 10 November.

title: Lunar Orbiter 2 Launches to Photograph the Moon
summary: On November 6, 1966, NASA launched Lunar Orbiter 2, a spacecraft built to photograph possible landing sites on the Moon.

body.text: A Survey of the Moon

NASA launched Lunar Orbiter 2 on November 6, 1966, on an Atlas-Agena D rocket. The spacecraft was designed mainly to photograph smooth areas of the lunar surface, so that safe landing sites could be chosen and checked for later missions. NASA's records say it returned 609 high-resolution and 208 medium-resolution frames, among them an oblique view of the crater Copernicus. After its photography and tracking work, it was crashed into the Moon on command on October 11, 1967, at about 3.0 degrees north and 119.1 degrees east.

title: The Kelly Barnes Dam Fails Above Toccoa Falls College
summary: At about 1:30 a.m. on November 6, 1977, the Kelly Barnes Dam in Toccoa, Georgia, failed after heavy rain, and the flood killed 39 people.

body.text: A Dam Fails in Georgia

The Kelly Barnes Dam, above Toccoa Falls College in Toccoa, Georgia, failed at about 1:30 a.m. on Sunday, November 6, 1977. The U.S. Geological Survey records roughly 7 inches of rain over the storm, including nearly 3.5 inches between 6 p.m. and midnight on November 5, after heavy rain on October 25 and 26. The dam was about 400 feet long and at most about 38 feet high, and its lake covered about 40 acres. The flood killed 39 people and covered part of the campus, including a trailer park. The investigating board could not name a single cause of the failure.
